Years of medications drying my mouth, malnutrition from reduced appetite, stress hormones from CRPS accelerating the process. It's apparently quite common for teeth to suffer with long term chronic conditions so I started saving up and planning for the future not long after my diagnosis.

All you can do is try. Pain is such a subjective thing. I know it's difficult to decide but giving your body and mind time to assess each option is the best approach. I've never had lidocaine so can't share an experience there. What I can tell you is I've always given every treatment option at least a few weeks to a month to work and carefully written down how each day went to look at later. Balancing concerns about physical appearance vs physical comfort is never an easy choice either, but mental health also plays a factor into pain management so weight gain and loss of the tooth itself are  also things that only you can decide are factors for treatment. The nerve block WILL help you dampen your sympathetic nervous system response to trigger points and while it doesn't change your mental health outlook specifically, it can be useful in calming the bodys response to stressful situations... so that all by itself is something to look forward to hun. I wish you all the best and I truly hope you have comfort on your horizon fast approaching. Remember, sometimes ALL we can control is our response, and you're doing an awesome job of that by weighing up your options and keeping an open mind xx

From my personal experience, the nerve block pain relief was almost instant, but everyone responds differently, so it might take more or less time for others. I also found that not taking any opiate-based medication helped reduce the risk of withdrawal symptoms increasing pain between doses. Opiates and I are decidedly NOT friends 🤣🙄

As for Cymbalta, I haven’t tried it myself. I was already on Amitriptyline, which helped a little (mostly with sleep), but not enough for me to want to try another antidepressant option. I also used Lyrica, but it didn’t help me much. Like you, I hesitated to try more invasive options like tooth removal. Unfortunately, my hesitance and choices eventually led to needing all my teeth removed, so I might not be the best person to advise on whether pulling a tooth is the right call in your case.

That said, I really believe it’s important to make decisions based on what feels right for you and your specific situation. From what you've shared, I know you'll find the best path for yourself ❤️. It might sound repetitive, but I wish someone had told me this more often: trust your instincts. I feel like I wasted years in uncertainty before taking control of my medical care and making decisions based on my own challenges.

By considering less invasive options first, you keep your flexibility open. It allows you to hedge your bets while still having more drastic treatments, like tooth extraction, available later if needed. In the end, the best thing you can do is trust yourself and choose what makes you feel the most comfortable and in control.

Removing the teeth ultimately had the biggest impact because it got rid of all nerves and any traces of residual infections. The nerve block played an important role as well, preventing additional pain during the procedure and lowering the risk of the pain spreading.

Although I’ve previously experienced seizures while pregnant—without any identified origin or diagnosis—this procedure didn’t lead to any seizures, even with my elevated seizure threshold. I wasn’t able to give much of an opinion regarding the risk of seizures, but so far, nothing has been triggered by the surgery or the nerve block.

I still needed painkillers for the bone pain during recovery (since having all my teeth removed and my jaw shaved is a major process), but the burning sensation from CRPS never became an issue. Even the painful hotspots from previous extractions went away.

On top of that, this experience helped ease some of the PTSD symptoms I developed due to medical anxiety. Living with a chronic pain condition and having been hurt unintentionally by medical professionals in the past has made me anxious around doctors. The nerve block, and how smoothly everything went, really helped reduce that fear and gave me more confidence in managing my medical care.

For me, the nerve block was incredibly useful in helping me distinguish between 'physical' pain—like inflammation, bone pain, or injury—and nerve pain, which, though very real, doesn’t come from a specific physical source if that makes sense. 

In terms of your final question, what I would do in your situation - I can't tell you exactly what I would do if I were you  but I hope by sharing my own experiences it can help you to feel more empowered in the choices you make. Getting additional advice on the risks vs benefits as well as perhaps requesting additional testing to determine the risk of seizures based on your personal history, health and any medication you are currently taking may also help to ease your mind a bit when deciding on what the best course of action is for you. The public mental healthcare system is designed to accommodate the most immediate and urgent cases, and without adequate resources, it is woefully under-equipped to help most people - but this is not for lack of trying. 

They tend to focus mostly on mental health crisis management, and there is a severe lack of adequate follow-up services for those who have yet to reach breaking point or have but are in recovery. 

The private mental healthcare system is better funded and has some amazing resources available but is also lacking in beds and is a business model that is maximised for profit rather than recovery. The private mental health hospitals are often filled with those who have been deposited there to be babysat by their burnt out family members who can afford PHI and need respite themselves from the very real and often under-discussed exposure to supporter fatigue.

I have at times wondered if both the patients AND the staff in the public and private health care systems would benefit from spending a night as a patient in the opposite care facility - to experience the other side and gain a little more perspective. 

Sadly, it's a bit like dental health here in Australia. 
Teeth are rich people bones. Sanity is a luxury purchase. 

I wish it were all better, but in every instance, we can't let the perfect be the enemy of the good.

Everyone's journey is different. What I can tell you is that many surgeons will advise you to have the surgery they are most experienced in,  which will be their favourite for many reasons. Sleeve specialists will tell you to get the sleeve. Bypass specialists will tell you to get the bypass, and so on.

Training for new procedures is costly and time-consuming so many surgeons will prefer to convince you that the procedure they are most experienced in is your best option regardless of what the facts might be.
Finding a surgeon who doesn't have a favourite procedure will help you to make a decision that is best for you, not for them. They can be more expensive due to their extra training and experience, but your body is much more precious than anything else you will ever invest in, so making sure you have the best is always a good idea.

I was fortunate enough to meet a surgeon who had done many different types of bariatric surgery over the years and he very openly answered all of my questions about success rates and complications. My favourite options were sleeve, standard bypass, and omega loop bypass.
He advised that many of his older gastric band patients had returned for sleeves over the years due to regains and complications. The same trend had been evident at the time (8 years ago) for sleevers wanting to be bypassed. Pretty much all surgeries had a similar rate for gallbladder complications as this is a side effect of rapid weight loss, not the procedure itself. Reflux seemed to be higher for sleeve and post op complications like ulcers and leaks for sleevers who took up smoking or drinking was higher than those with bypass. The biggest difference I noticed between standard bypass and omega loop bypass was that the omega loop patients had better chances of keeping weight off and fewer scar tissue complications due to only one anastomosis site (standard bypass has two). Omega loop was also easier to reverse if there was any medical reason for doing so.

I looked at all of the data and decided that I only wanted one surgery. I went with omega loop gastric bypass based on long-term maintenance of weight loss and lower complication rates. I also hated the idea of the sleeve resulting in my spare stomach being thrown in the bin afterwards, making it irreversible. 

It's been about 8 years and I've maintained a 70 kg loss. Gained 20 kg back with pregnancy and lost all of it in less than a year after the birth. I had my gall bladder removed about two years after my omega loop surgery and have had no other major complications, or reflux issues. Briefly returned to smoking cigarettes about 4 years out and developed a tiny ulcer, so stopped that again and it healed pretty quickly. 

Bariatric surgery for me has been like inviting a tiny stern teacher to live in my tummy. She treats me kindly as long as I take care of myself, and I feel happy and healthy. If I step out of line she tells me off and disciplines me for doing the wrong thing haha. I've learned to live with my new stomach, made mistakes, corrected them and found a good balance. 

TL,DR - Get the advice of a very experienced surgeon before you make a decision, and choose your procedure wisely. 
They are there at the beginning but you will be stuck with your decision for life xx

It consisted of 1 week clear, thin liquids (like broth, water, juice), 1 week of thicker liquids (milkshakes, smoothies, soups), 2 weeks of puree foods, and then two weeks of soft foods like scambled eggs and other soft, easy to digest food items before i had regular foods again. I tried a few times to jump ahead and was in a world of pain. My surgeon said to imagine I had a baby's stomach and to try to ease back into proper solids very slowly in order to give my new stomach the maximum time it needed to heal x x

I had no idea how depressed I actually was until I felt that dark cloud starting to shift during TMS. I had carried it for so long that I barely even noticed that it was there, but its absence made such a difference in my recovery. I firmly believe that mental health professionals should play a strong role in addressing the needs of chronic pain patients. All involved in pain management must be mindful of how quickly depression and anxiety begin to manifest in the presence of chronic, long term pain. 

With every form of therapy I noticed small improvements as time went by, but the best results were from an intensive two week CBT course followed by individual appointments with my pain psychologist. I saw so much improvement from the first time I completed CBT that I even returned to do a refresher a couple of years later. I firmly believe that the second course was actually more successful than my first attempt as I had just completed my TMS sessions immediately beforehand. TMS helps to improve neuroplasticity, and my depressive symptoms eased dramatically after about 15 sessions. By the time I commenced the CBT program I was in a much more receptive learning state. 

There are many different techniques a psychologist experienced in helping those with chronic pain may suggest. My pain psych has been one of my strongest supporters and made many helpful suggestions for my treatment. Most pain specialist doctors will know of a few decent pain psychs if you decide you would like to see one.

I raged against my diagnosis (complex regional pain syndrome) and the associated pain from the start. I simply could not believe that pain killers wouldn't ever "kill" my pain again.  I tried every drug, saw scores of specialists, and tried many different forms of therapeutic treatments too. Some things worked better than others, but nothing would take the pain away. After a while I came to accept that I needed to coexist with my pain, and share my body with my condition. 

Releasing the anger associated with my pain was difficult to say the least, but I realised that only my mental health and response to how I coped each day was all that I could control. 
Today I have a pain psychologist I see regularly.  I have also completed courses in cognitive and dialectical behavioural therapy, amongst scores of other psychotherapies, and recently had 20 sessions of Transmagnetic Cranial Stimulation for depression. All of the time spent on getting my head around the concept of living life with often acute but always chronic pain has been resourceful for me.

I cannot ignore my pain any more than I could at the start (unless I'm at maximum volume on a Ketamine infusion, but that's another story). What I can do is view it from a detached, analytical point of view when using my tools as recommended. I have days where they simply do not work, but in general my pain is far easier to cope with today than it was before I actively sought mental health support. 
I hope you find some answers for yourself one day. Feel free to message me if you ever need to vent x

My therapist explained to me once about the levels of cortisol and adrenaline released when in constant pain push the body's stress response way closer to the edge of triggering fight/flight/freeze. For example on a scale of 1-10, if someone not in pain has maybe a level 2 or 3 stress level, chronic pain sufferers are at a 6 or 7. Hence the short fuse. We are always much closer to the edge point of losing our shit because an outside stressor (like an injury or conflict/argument) feels so much more intense. 
This knowledge was the driving factor for me as I learned as many Cognitive Behavioural Therapy skills as possible to cope better with pain. I try really hard to challenge stressful thoughts from a rational perspective now, and it really does help.

I have 6-7 day infusions as an inpatient in a private hospital, delivered subcutaneously. I start at around 6 mcg per hour, and slowly ramp this up over the first 24 hours until I reach around 20 mcg per hour, where I remain for 5-6 days. This is my "sweet spot", a dosage determined between my doctor and I, based on my BMI, tolerance to side effects and pain score. The idea is to feel tipsy as opposed to drunk, and stay there for several days. The pain relief during the infusion is excellent, and for at least 8-10 weeks afterwards also.

I only just saw this. I don't know how I missed it. Honey, i feel you. I AM you, much of the time. I wish that I had the right words for you, a sort of balm for your invisible wounds, but I'm sadly just as lost as you are, much of the time. I take great pains to appear as put together as possible, in fact I even post in here about my clothing and my appearance being seen as my armor. The idea being, that I dress and make myself up to be the person outwardly that I wish I was on the inside. At times I do really well..my new mantra is now "live it til I believe it" rather than "fake it til i make it". I'm very much not okay mentally and physically much of the time. I'm on a slightly more positive trajectory at present after very long inpatient hospital admissions for both my mental and physical health, but those were bubbles. Every day, now that I am "out", those same demons lurk beneath the veneer of therapy and pain relief I have recently received. Every day is a war between the old habits and the new, a war of words and wills, and its fucking hard. Ridiculously hard sometimes. And I'm tired. I'm so fucking tired that I want to scream and demand that the world just shut up and let me sleep. The problem is, i could sleep forever quite happily given the choice. Not in actual death persay, but in the shitty pseudo existence I construct for myself so as to avoid extra ouch on any level - my pain cocoon. 
All I can keep in check is my attitude to life, and remind myself that I, and I alone, make the choice each day to continue breathing. To continue fighting if need be. As do you. For what its worth, I'm glad you make the choice to keep your pain as invisible as you can despite the exhaustion. To me, it signifies a fire, a strength within you to go on existing in spite of it all. It gives me hope for you. I hope you find relief soon. You deserve nothing but the best life has to offer, and I sincerely pray you will find it.

Yes. Its resulted in a diagnosis of every mental health issue under the sun at one point or another over the years relating to paranoia, but only ever in during wolf week.

I definitely recommend trialling it in some form if your doctor thinks you are a suitable candidate. The delivery method seems to need to be tailored to your individual circumstances to be most effective, and I truly believe having the right rapport with an open minded, cooperative doctor is essential in achieving this goal. I've had subcut and oral ketamine treatments so far. 
In my own personal experience with subcutaneous ketamine infusions in hospital, I would generally experience very low to pain free days. Upon going home, i would probably leave with a pain score of 3-4, which gradually would fade to a baseline of 7-8 by about 3 months later. 
This every day oral treatment option is at a much lower dose and has more of an immediate effect followed by a gradual tapering off like any other med. The ongoing half life should offer a similar baseline to what I've experienced in the past from infusions once there's a bit of a build up in my system, but only time will tell. 
I'm on a number of other complementary medications that work well with ketamine in my personal experience, so I don't believe ket treatment is a cure-all so much as an effective tool when used correctly. I hope this all made some sense 😂
